newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian brewers fight wine invasion.
newsitem.headline: Australian brewers fight wine invasion.

text.p: Former prime minister Bob Hawke, whose legendary drinking once landed him in the Guinness Book of Records, was once the epitome of the beer-loving Australian male.
But Hawke's decision in 1980 to swear off alcohol to pursue his dream of leading Australia has been reflected in a dramatic change in the country's drinking habits.

Twenty years ago Australians drank 136 litres (30 gallons) of beer per person each year, putting them near the top of the world rankings and attesting to a cultural history which saw Hawke enter the record books in the 1950s by draining a yard of ale in 11 seconds.

Now per capita beer consumption is down to about 95 litres (21 gallons) a year and is pushing the nation's two major brewers -- New Zealand-based Lion Nathan and Foster's Carlton and United Beer (CUB) -- to find new ways and new products to keep Australians drinking their beloved amber fluid.
While the majority of Australians did not follow Hawke "on the wagon", to swear off alcohol, industry sources say they now drink less, but better quality, beer.
The decline in beer consumption is a trend shared by many Western nations, including Britain and the United States, and is driven by social and health pressures.
In Australia it also reflects changes in the ethnic make-up of the country, with a post-World War Two flood of European migrants producing a sophisticated wine industry.

Stephen Couche from wine producer Orlando Wyndham, owned by the French Pernod Ricard group, told a recent wine conference that Australian wine drinking changed in the mid-1960s, when consumption was only six litres (1.3 gallons) a head per year and a bottle of beer was the centrepiece of any social event.
NEW TREND

"The more progressive hotels around the country were in full swing with a novel new trend called counter meals and sharing a bottle of sparkling wine (white or pink) with a solid 'roast of the day' broke new ground," Couche said.

European migrants stimulated an appreciation of Mediterranean cuisine, he added, driving a growing interest in wine particularly as a companion to food. Wine consumption per head rose to around 18 litres (four gallons) by 1990.
Domestic wine consumption has stalled in the last five years. Industry sources say this was mainly to meet demand from export markets that have grown more than 22 percent a year since 1990.
But marketing forecasters BIS Shrapnel recently predicted beer will continue to lose market share to wine and spirits.

Analyst Sandro Mangosi attributed this redistribution to increasing multicultural influences, particularly the number of ethnic restaurants, the ageing of the population, declining numbers of blue-collar workers, and drink-driving restrictions.

"People are drinking less at lunch time, more with meals and less without meals, and they are drinking 'better' as they are choosing their drinks with greater care and moving upmarket in their choice of wines and spirits," Mangosi said.

The two major beer companies have taken the hint and, while competing aggressively for the remaining traditional beer market -- CUB has a 55 percent share to Lion's 42 percent -- they are looking for growth and higher margins from premium beers.
The bid is to get beer back onto the dining table.
GOOD MARKETING
Both companies admit the wine industry has marketed itself well as the cheap drink through a lower tax base and the premium choice that even beer drinkers accept for meals.
"Our goal really is not to get people drinking more beer, but getting more people drinking beer on more occasions," Chuck Hahn, chief brewer with Lion Nathan recently told Reuters.

Lion and CUB both have launched major marketing drives to promote beer as the choice for many meals, particularly hotter, spicier Asian dishes, issuing recipes and food guides and printing beer-based menus for pub-restaurants.
The brewers say they do not expect a short-term resurgence, but they believe the decline of beer has bottomed due to moves to different types of beer and combined promotions of beer and food.
